content: 1. In settings with a high risk of tuberculosis exposure, all infants should receive a single dose of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. 2. Communication and play should be actively encouraged in neonatal care. 3. Preterm and low-birth-weight infants must be identified immediately after birth and provided with specialized care in accordance with existing WHO guidelines. 4. Neonatal vitamin A supplementation within the first 28 days of life is not recommended as a public health intervention to reduce infant morbidity and mortality. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate evidence for mortality-related outcomes. 5. For term or preterm newborns requiring positive-pressure ventilation, the umbilical cord should be clamped and cut to facilitate effective ventilation. This is a weak recommendation based on consensus in the absence of published evidence. 6. Newborns who do not breathe spontaneously after thorough drying should be stimulated by rubbing their back 2–3 times before clamping the cord and initiating positive-pressure ventilation. This is a weak recommendation based on consensus in the absence of published evidence. 7. Suctioning of the mouth and nose is not necessary for neonates born through clear amniotic fluid who begin breathing on their own after birth. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 8. For neonates born through clear amniotic fluid who do not start breathing after thorough drying and back stimulation, routine suctioning of the mouth and nose before initiating positive-pressure ventilation is not recommended. Suctioning should only be performed if there are visible secretions in the mouth or nose. This is a weak recommendation based on consensus in the absence of published evidence. 9. In cases of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, intrapartum suctioning of the mouth and nose at the delivery of the head is not recommended. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 10. Tracheal suctioning is not recommended for neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who start breathing on their own. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate to low-quality evidence. 11. For neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who do not start breathing on their own, tracheal suctioning should be performed before initiating positive-pressure ventilation if endotracheal intubation is possible. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 12. In resource-limited settings where mechanical suction equipment is unavailable, a bulb syringe (single-use or easy-to-clean) is preferred over a mucus extractor with a trap for suctioning newborns. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 13. Positive-pressure ventilation should be initiated within one minute of birth for newborns who do not start breathing despite thorough drying and additional stimulation. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 14. For term or preterm newborns (>32 weeks gestation) requiring positive-pressure ventilation, ventilation should be initiated with air rather than pure oxygen. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 15. Positive-pressure ventilation in newborns should be provided using a self-inflating bag and mask. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 16. Ventilation in newborns requiring positive-pressure ventilation should be initiated using a face-mask interface. This is a strong recommendation based on limited availability and lack of experience with nasal cannulae, despite low evidence for benefits. 17. The adequacy of ventilation in newborns should be assessed by measuring the heart rate after 60 seconds of ventilation with visible chest movements. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 18. For newborns who do not start breathing within one minute after birth, priority should be given to providing adequate ventilation rather than chest compressions. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 19. Resuscitation should be stopped in newborns with no detectable heart rate after 10 minutes of effective ventilation. This is a weak recommendation relevant to resource-limited settings, based on very low-quality evidence. 20. Resuscitation should also be stopped in newborns who continue to have a heart rate below 60 beats per minute and no spontaneous breathing after 20 minutes of resuscitation. This is a weak recommendation relevant to resource-limited settings, based on very low-quality evidence. 21. Head or whole-body cooling should not be performed outside well-resourced tertiary neonatal intensive care units due to the potential for harm in low-resource settings. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 22. Neonates born to mothers with prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours), maternal fever (>38°C), or foul-smelling/purulent amniotic fluid should be treated with prophylactic antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) for at least two days. After two days, treatment should continue only if there are signs of sepsis or a positive blood culture. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 23. Neonates with signs of sepsis should be treated with ampicillin (or penicillin) and gentamicin as first-line antibiotic therapy for at least 10 days. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 24. If neonates with sepsis show extensive skin pustules, abscesses, or omphalitis, they should be treated with cloxacillin and gentamicin instead of penicillin and gentamicin. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is not graded. 25. Blood cultures should be obtained before starting antibiotics whenever possible. If the infant does not improve within 2–3 days, antibiotic treatment should be changed, or the infant should be referred for further management. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is not graded. 26. Community health workers conducting home visits as part of postnatal care should counsel families on recognizing danger signs, assess young infants for danger signs of illness, and promote appropriate care-seeking. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 27. Young infants aged 0–6 days with fast breathing as the only sign of illness should be referred to a hospital. If referral is not feasible, they should be treated with oral amoxicillin (50 mg/kg per dose, twice daily for seven days) by a trained health worker. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 28. Young infants aged 7–59 days with fast breathing as the only sign of illness should be treated with oral amoxicillin (50 mg/kg per dose, twice daily for seven days) by a trained health worker. Referral is not necessary. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 29. Low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, including very low-birth-weight (VLBW) infants, should be fed with their mother’s own milk. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 30. If mother’s milk is unavailable, LBW and VLBW infants should be fed donor human milk, provided safe and affordable milk-banking facilities are available. This is a strong situational recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 31. If neither mother’s milk nor donor human milk is available, LBW and VLBW infants should be fed standard infant formula. This is a weak situational recommendation relevant to resource-limited settings, based on low-quality evidence.
